doc.title: Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 30, 1995

title: Bass lineage: Blanton, Slam Stewart, Pettiford, Chambers, Carter
summary: Cobb and Booker trace bass history from Jimmy Blanton through Slam Stewart and Pettiford to Paul Chambers and Ron Carter; Booker says he came out sounding like Pettiford.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Give us a quick chronology of who you think some of the bass lineage is. We talked about Hawkins and Prez and Bird and Trane. Give us some of that bass chronology then.
You have to start out with Jimmy Blanton.
Absolutely.
Yeah ‘cause he’s the one who kind of modernized that bass playing, because before then they was playing [scats], like two beat notes. He kind of started to play the chord and walk changes.
Yeah he played melodic lines, but in harmony within what the changes are. Plus he played great solos huh?
Oh he played great solos.
Plus he could play with the bow. And Duke Ellington loved him. He could play melodies, I don’t know if you know it was a duo thing with him.

He was a well trained bass player. Like maybe he trained, I don’t know whether he trained for the symphony or not, but he was probably taught that way, or somebody taught him that, or either the gift came, from where it comes from. And nobody have to teach you nothing then, you know, it’s there.
And what about his partner?
Oh, Slam Stewart.
See people may not give him credit because it was such a commercial kind of thing that he sang and played, but—
Oh, he was a killer man.
He was a very unbelievable— © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
A very unbelievable bass player.
And so then, there are so many great guys.
Then there was Oscar Pettiford came in off of the top of that.

Which I sort of started from there in my — I don’t know that I consciously liked him, because I would like concentrate on all kinds of other people but I came out sounding like that. When I first heard myself play, I said, I don’t want to sound— I mean I didn’t mean I don’t want to — is that me I said. But anyway, I think that’s where I really came from.
Then there was Paul Chambers. Young Paul Chambers. He came like he sounded like he was the extension off of both of them guys.
Yeah he means Jimmy Blanton and Oscar Pettiford.

He sounded like he was an extension, the modern extension of those guys. You know and then there’s guys, there’s Ron Carter. But now there’s a host of young guys that’s in that idiom you know, killers. They’re really bad.
